title: The Major Currencies and What They Are Used For
intro: Each major currency has a role in the world economy that shapes how it behaves: the dollar as the world's money, the yen and Swiss franc as funding currencies and safe havens, the Australian and Canadian dollars as bets on commodities. Knowing these roles explains much of what currencies do in calm markets and in crises.

items: On one side of almost 90% of all FX trades (BIS 2022 survey; each trade has two sides, so shares add to 200%).
About 57 to 59% of the world's disclosed foreign exchange reserves held by central banks in recent IMF COFER data, down from about 70% around 2000 but still far ahead of the euro's roughly 20%.
The currency in which oil and most commodities are priced, and in which a large share of world trade and cross-border loans are invoiced.

US Treasuries are the deepest safe asset in the world, so in a global crisis the dollar usually rises as everyone scrambles for dollars to repay dollar debts (the 'dollar smile': the dollar is strong when the world is in crisis and when the US economy leads, weaker in between).
The Federal Reserve provides swap lines to other central banks in crises (2008, 2020) so that dollar shortages abroad don't spiral.
Being the reserve currency lets the US borrow cheaply in its own currency, a privilege a French finance minister called 'exorbitant' in the 1960s.

blocks.text: The euro has been the currency of most of the European Union since 1999 (notes and coins from 2002), now used by 20 countries, with monetary policy set by the European Central Bank. It is the second reserve and second most traded currency. Its quirk is a single central bank with many separate national governments and bond markets, which produced the 2010-2012 euro debt crisis, when Greek, Irish, Portuguese, Spanish and Italian borrowing costs soared until ECB President Mario Draghi pledged to do 'whatever it takes' (July 2012). Denmark's krone is pegged to the euro within a narrow band.
Japanese yen (JPY): the funding currency and safe haven

items: Japan has had very low interest rates since the 1990s, zero or negative for most of 2016 to 2024. That makes the yen cheap to borrow, so it is the classic funding currency for the carry trade: borrow yen at near zero, sell them, and buy higher-yielding assets (US Treasuries, Australian or Mexican deposits, stocks).

Japan is one of the world's largest net creditors: its households, companies and institutions own far more foreign assets than foreigners own of Japan. In a crisis, Japanese investors bring money home and carry trades are closed, both of which mean buying yen, so the yen tends to rise when markets fall: a safe haven.

The two roles collide in a carry unwind. On 31 July 2024 the Bank of Japan raised rates and the yen jumped; leveraged carry positions were closed in a rush and on 5 August 2024 the Nikkei 225 fell 12.4%, its worst day since 1987. In 2008 the yen rose about 20% against the dollar as carry trades collapsed.
The Japanese Ministry of Finance intervenes when moves are 'excessive', most recently selling dollars to support a weak yen in 2022 and 2024.

blocks.text: Sterling is the oldest currency in continuous use and fourth most traded. The UK's large financial sector and its current account deficit (it relies on foreign capital) make the pound sensitive to confidence. Notable episodes: Black Wednesday in September 1992, when the pound was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (George Soros's fund reportedly made about \$1 billion betting against it); the fall of more than 10% after the June 2016 Brexit vote; and the 2022 'mini-budget' crisis, when GBP/USD briefly touched about 1.035, a record low.
Swiss franc (CHF): the other safe haven

Switzerland combines political neutrality, a long record of low inflation, a large current account surplus and huge foreign assets, so money flows into the franc in times of fear. Like the yen, it has had very low or negative rates and has been used to fund borrowing: in the 2000s many households in Poland, Hungary and Austria took Swiss-franc mortgages for their lower rates, then suffered when the franc rose.

To stop the franc's rise, the Swiss National Bank set a floor of 1.20 francs per euro in September 2011 and bought euros without limit to defend it. On 15 January 2015 it abandoned the floor without warning: the franc jumped about 30% within minutes before settling some 15 to 20% higher, several FX brokers were bankrupted by customer losses, and traders who had treated the floor as a guarantee learned that a peg is only as good as the central bank's willingness to defend it.
Commodity currencies: AUD, CAD, NZD, NOK

items: Australian dollar (AUD, the 'Aussie'): Australia exports iron ore, coal and natural gas, much of it to China, so the AUD tracks commodity prices and Chinese growth. Historically higher interest rates made it a favorite carry-trade target; AUD/JPY is watched as a gauge of global risk appetite.
Canadian dollar (CAD): tied to oil and to the US economy, which buys about three-quarters of Canada's exports.
New Zealand dollar (NZD): dairy and farm exports; another high-yield carry target.
Norwegian krone (NOK): oil and gas; Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest, invests oil revenue abroad.

blocks.text: The renminbi ('people's currency', unit yuan) is managed: each morning the People's Bank of China sets a central parity ('the fix') against the dollar, and onshore trading (CNY) may move up to 2% either side of it. Capital controls limit money flowing in and out. An offshore market in Hong Kong and elsewhere (CNH) trades more freely, usually close to CNY. The yuan joined the IMF's SDR basket in 2016 and is growing in trade settlement, but remains a small share of reserves (about 2%).

items: Hong Kong dollar: pegged to the US dollar since 1983 through a currency board, within 7.75 to 7.85 per dollar.
Gulf currencies: the Saudi riyal (3.75 per dollar since 1986) and others are pegged to the dollar, which suits economies that sell oil priced in dollars.
Mexican peso (MXN): liquid and higher-yielding, a popular carry-trade target in recent years.

Brazilian real, South African rand, Turkish lira, Indian rupee, Indonesian rupiah and others: higher interest rates, higher inflation and larger swings. Currency crises (Mexico 1994, Asia 1997, Russia 1998, Argentina repeatedly, Turkey 2018 and 2021) often come when a country with dollar debts and a falling currency finds the debts growing in local terms.

blocks.text: Gold was the anchor of the monetary system under the gold standard and Bretton Woods (until the US ended dollar convertibility in 1971); central banks still hold it as a reserve asset and have bought heavily since 2022. It trades as XAU against the dollar. Bitcoin and other crypto assets are traded like currencies but are too volatile to serve as money for most uses; stablecoins are tokens backed by dollar assets. See Real Estate, Commodities and Alternatives.

blocks.title: Safe-haven logic
blocks.text: A sudden global stock market crash begins. Which way would you expect USD/JPY and AUD/JPY to move, and why?
solution: Both are likely to fall, meaning the yen strengthens: carry trades funded in yen are closed (buying back yen) and Japanese investors repatriate money. AUD/JPY usually falls further than USD/JPY, because the AUD is a risk-sensitive commodity currency while the dollar itself is a haven.

blocks.title: A peg's risk
blocks.text: In 2014 a trader held €1 million of short CHF/long EUR exposure (long EUR/CHF), believing the 1.20 floor made losses impossible. EUR/CHF moved from 1.20 to about 1.04 after the floor was removed. Roughly what was the loss in francs?
solution: Loss $\approx 1{,}000{,}000 \times (1.20 - 1.04) = 160{,}000$ francs, about 13% of the position; with 20× leverage that would be more than the trader's whole account.
